Definition
In this lesson, you will learn about the circuits that make up a microwave transmitter.
INTRODUCTIONM
The purpose of a microwave communication system is to:
Process, Transmit, Receive and Interface Information to the user.
The transmitter section contains: Information Processor, Oscillator & Modulator, Transmitter, Waveguide System and Antenna System................
These sections are common to all microwave transmitters; however, the circuits used can be different.
Let's begin the lesson on MICROWAVE TRANSMITTERS..........................
LESSON MENU
MICROWAVE TRANSMITTERS
This is a block diagram of a typical microwave transmitter.
DISCUSSION
At first glance, it may appear that it does not contain all the necessary stages that a transmitter must have.
But it does! Let's cover each stage starting with the information processor.
* Information Processor * Oscillator/Modulator
The information processor makes the information suitable for transmission.
The audio amplifier, audio oscillator and the external input make up the information processor in this basic system.
Either an external signal (any type of signal, multiplexed or not) or the output of the audio oscillator (used if an external signal is not available) is routed to the audio amplifier.
The audio amplifier boosts the signal and sends it to the DRO as a modulation signal.
The oscillator/modulator is contained on the waveguide system.
* Information Processor * Oscillator/Modulator
The oscillator is located in the DRO and generates the microwave frequency.
Power for the DRO is applied from the power supply.
The modulator is also located in the DRO and modulates the carrier frequency with the signal output from the audio amplifier.
The entire diagram is normally considered the transmitter.
* Information Processor * Oscillator/Modulator
However, it is the DRO that funnels the modulated microwave frequency down the waveguide to the antenna.
The waveguide system receives the modulated RF energy from the DRO and passes it to the antenna.
* Information Processor * Oscillator/Modulator
Waveguides are used as conductors when the RF is in the microwave range due to high losses of wire conductors.
The antenna system directs the microwave energy to the receiver.
* Information Processor * Oscillator/Modulator

6 VDC and a variable positive 8 to 12 VDC.
IC5 is a variable regulator that produces 8 to 12 VDC for the DRO. R19 controls the output voltage.
TP5 is used for monitoring the DRO voltage and J2 is the PC card connector.
CR3 and CR4 are zener diode regulators that produce the 6 VDC used to supply power to the audio amplifier.
Test points are provided to monitor the 6 VDC.
The 15 VDC input power is also used as power to the audio oscillator. Test points for monitoring are provided.
The audio oscillator circuit is formed by IC1, IC2 and IC3.
IC1 produces two outputs, a sine wave and a triangular wave at
IC2 and IC3 are operational amplifiers for the two outputs of IC1. Power for IC1 and IC2 is
Output test points are provided using the waveform symbol for identification.
IC4 is an audio amplifier with an output gain control and DC offset control. Power for IC4 is
The input to the audio amplifier is either the external input or the sine wave output of IC2. S1 selects the input.
Notice that S1 is also used on the output of IC4. Selection is either the output of IC4 or the triangular wave.
The PC card output is routed to the DRO as a modulation signal via J1. TP4 is used to monitor the output signal.
The external input signal is limited by CR1 and CR2, and filtered by C3 and C4. This forms the low pass filter.
The low pass filter allows frequencies between 50 Hz and 6 MHz to pass. The external input can be audio, video, digital or a combination of all three.
Notice that C3 and C4 block frequencies less than 50 Hz, also performing as coupling capacitors in block DC current flow.
Remember, different microwave transmitters may use different circuits. This is a typical circuit.
